ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Three subjects were not included due to having less than 50 total assessments (distinctively fewer than all other subjects), and one subject was not included due to subsequent missing values over a week.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Three subjects were not included due to having less than 50 total assessments (distinctively fewer than all other subjects), and one subject was not included due to subsequent missing values over a week.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Mental Health and Social Contact During the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
table.description: This is the permanent, frozen registry of data, code, & measures for our manuscript in Clinical Psychological Science.

report: We found 1 preregistration. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(id = "erp7v", title = "Mental Health and Social Contact During the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study", template = "Open-Ended Registration"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 2, FALSE) ``` Meta-scientific research has shown that deviations from preregistrations are often not reported or checked, and that the most common deviations concern the sample size. For educational material on how to report deviations from preregistrations, see: Lakens, Daniël (2024). “When and How to Deviate From a Preregistration.” Collabra: Psychology, 10(1), 117094. doi:10.1525/collabra.117094. :::

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 77 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  24 of 1108 data columns (2%) are documented in a codebook; 1084 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (77 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 2% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `ID`, `DeviceID`, `Scheduled` while the data has `ID`, `Scheduled`, `Issued`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 6 codebook/README/label sources and 1108 data columns across 10 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (77 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 2% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents `ID`, `DeviceID`, `Scheduled` while the data has `ID`, `Scheduled`, `Issued`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

::: {.panel-tabset}

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1108 columns across 10 data files.
#### Issues Identified

26 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

110 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **52 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 8 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  8 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  4 of 8 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable (not counted against the traffic light).
-  29 installable dependencies detected.
- 1405 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 1 reported test matched (0%).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 8 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:8, File = c("2. Timeseries.R", "3. Network models.R", 
"4. Compare pre-post.R", "5. COVID cases NL.R", "6. Multilevel regression.R", 
"Supplementary Appendix R -script empiric example.R", "Supplementary Appendix R -script numerical examples.R", 
"Supplementary Appendix R -script var_ccov_decompose.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "none", "none", "none"
)), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `Fried_2022 data/clean_network.RData` to `../Archive of OSF Storage/4. Data/clean_network.RData` (in Supplementary Appendix R -script empiric example.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
They also run 1 script that is not in the deposit: `supplementary appendix r -script var_dcf_compare.r`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 4 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `6. Multilevel regression.R` (clean_network.RData). Then this one ran to the end: `6. Multilevel regression.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **3 scripts looked for 3 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `4. Data/clean_ema.RData` to `Archive of OSF Storage/5. Code/data/clean_ema.RData` for `2. Timeseries.R`; `4. Data/clean_network.RData` to `Archive of OSF Storage/5. Code/data/clean_network.RData` for `3. Network models.R`; `4. Data/clean_prepost.RData` to `Archive of OSF Storage/5. Code/data/clean_prepost.RData` for `4. Compare pre-post.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("2. Timeseries.R", "3. Network models.R", 
"4. Compare pre-post.R", "5. COVID cases NL.R", "6. Multilevel regression.R", 
"Supplementary Appendix R -script empiric example.R", "Supplementary Appendix R -script numerical examples.R", 
"Supplementary Appendix R -script var_ccov_decompose.R"), Outcome = c("errored", 
"errored", "ran_ok", "errored", "ran_ok", "dependency_unavailable", 
"ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("runtime", "runtime", "", "runtime", 
"", "dependency_unavailable", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(6.5, 4.7, 
6.2, 1.8, 243.4, 7.3, 7.2, 2.5)), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplementary Appendix R -script empiric example.R"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

13 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

The high covariance amongst observed psychopathologies requires an explanation and has implications for improving mental health interventions (Krueger & Eaton, 2015).
text.formatted: The high covariance amongst observed psychopathologies requires an explanation and has implications for improving mental health interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Krueger & Eaton, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The traditional categorical approach, which groups symptoms into discrete disorders, does not provide a satisfactory explanation for this covariance, or "comorbidity" (e.g., Kotov et al., 2017; Lilienfeld & Treadway, 2016).
text.formatted: The traditional categorical approach, which groups symptoms into discrete disorders, does not provide a satisfactory explanation for this covariance, or "comorbidity" (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kotov et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Lilienfeld & Treadway, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, other conceptualizations of psychopathology have gained popularity (N. R. Eaton et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Consequently, other conceptualizations of psychopathology have gained popularity (N. R. <ref type="bibr">Eaton et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the field of psychometrics, the best-known approaches are the common factor (CF) models and the symptom network (SN) models (Borsboom, 2017; Caspi et al., 2014; Cramer et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In the field of psychometrics, the best-known approaches are the common factor (CF) models and the symptom network (SN) models <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Caspi et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Cramer et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In their simplest form, CF models explain the symptom co-occurrence with a shared unobserved cause for multiple symptoms, traditionally viewed as a defining trait of the disorder or liability to it (Hopwood et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In their simplest form, CF models explain the symptom co-occurrence with a shared unobserved cause for multiple symptoms, traditionally viewed as a defining trait of the disorder or liability to it <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Hopwood et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, SN models explain the co-occurrence with causal effects between symptoms themselves.
In this way, the models have a distinct causal interpretation (Marsman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In this way, the models have a distinct causal interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Marsman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Stated as a counterargument to the CF models (Cramer et al., 2010), SN models dismiss the idea of an underlying shared cause and instead propose that psychopathology is n emergent feature arising from the causal effects between symptoms (Borsboom, 2017).
text.formatted: Stated as a counterargument to the CF models <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Cramer et al., 2010)</ref>, SN models dismiss the idea of an underlying shared cause and instead propose that psychopathology is n emergent feature arising from the causal effects between symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: That is, for the CF model the construct we are trying to capture is a common cause, while for the SN model the construct is the collection of symptoms and their mutual relationships (Rhemtulla et al., 2020).
text.formatted: That is, for the CF model the construct we are trying to capture is a common cause, while for the SN model the construct is the collection of symptoms and their mutual relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Rhemtulla et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: While both of the psychometric approaches are widely used (Hopwood et al., 2023; Robinaugh et al., 2020), concerns remain about whether the theory development has become stagnant: It is often implicitly assumed that the other approach is false, without evidence to justify the made assumption (Fried, 2020).
text.formatted: While both of the psychometric approaches are widely used <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Hopwood et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Robinaugh et al., 2020)</ref>, concerns remain about whether the theory development has become stagnant: It is often implicitly assumed that the other approach is false, without evidence to justify the made assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Fried, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One reason for this is that, despite being distinct in their causal interpretation, CF and SN models cannot, in general, be statistically distinguished from each other in cross-sectional data (Epskamp, Kruis, et al., 2017; Molenaar et al., 2007; but see Van Bork et al., 2021).
text.formatted: One reason for this is that, despite being distinct in their causal interpretation, CF and SN models cannot, in general, be statistically distinguished from each other in cross-sectional data <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Epskamp, Kruis, et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Molenaar et al., 2007</ref>; but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Van Bork et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This hinders direct empirical comparisons: when multiple models fit the data equally well, it becomes inherently difficult to discern which one more accurately captures the underlying psychological processes.

Especially, due to the arguable absence of well-defined interventions to evaluate theories in psychological research (Eronen, 2020) the importance of statistical comparisons, and so statistical distinguishability, is of interest.
text.formatted: Especially, due to the arguable absence of well-defined interventions to evaluate theories in psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Eronen, 2020)</ref> the importance of statistical comparisons, and so statistical distinguishability, is of interest.

text.text: Statistical distinguishability means the distribution of symptoms being different under substantively distinct models, which are in our case SN and CF models (Spirtes et al., 2000, pp. 59-72).
text.formatted: Statistical distinguishability means the distribution of symptoms being different under substantively distinct models, which are in our case SN and CF models <ref type="bibr">(Spirtes et al., 2000, pp. 59-72)</ref>.

text.text: That is, indistinguishable models predict equal distribution for the modelled variables.
A weaker version can be defined as distinguishability in covariance.

We will mainly use this weaker definition throughout the article, as covariance-based analysis is the most common approach in applied empirical studies of this field and suffices to show the main point, but we will also generalise to distributional distinguishability.
From here on we use (in)distinguishability as shorthand for covariance distinguishability, if not otherwise specified.

To date, for the CF and SN models the discussion on distinguishability is limited to crosssectional results indicating indistinguishability in covariance (Molenaar et al., 2007; Van Bork et al., 2021) and cross-sectional item response theory models (Marsman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: To date, for the CF and SN models the discussion on distinguishability is limited to crosssectional results indicating indistinguishability in covariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Molenaar et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Van Bork et al., 2021)</ref> and cross-sectional item response theory models <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Marsman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Stationary dynamic CF models, presented as an autoregressive model in an augmented vectorfoot_0 have been discussed in at least two occasions (Molenaar, 1985; Stock & Watson, 2005).
text.formatted: Stationary dynamic CF models, presented as an autoregressive model in an augmented vector<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> have been discussed in at least two occasions <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Molenaar, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Stock & Watson, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Though, no direct analysis of distinguishability was done in either study.
An adjacent topic in time series literature is singular autoregression models (Anderson et al., 2012; Deistler et al., 2010). 3 These models have reduced rank innovation covariance.
text.formatted: An adjacent topic in time series literature is singular autoregression models <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Deistler et al., 2010)</ref>. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">3</ref> These models have reduced rank innovation covariance.

text.text: As we will show below, reduced rank innovation covariance is a necessary but insufficient condition for indistinguishability between a longitudinal SN and a CF model.

Moreover, a thorough analysis mindful of contemporaneous psychopathology research would account for i) the data being possibly ordinal and conflated with measurement error, ii) the plausibility of non-normal distributions in psychopathology (Reise et al., 2018; Talkkari & Rosenström, 2024), iii) that psychopathology develops continuously in time (for example, Kuiper & Ryan, 2018; Ryan & Hamaker, 2022) and iv) the psychopathology process being non-stationary (Bringmann, 2021; Schumacher et al., 2023; Siepe et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, a thorough analysis mindful of contemporaneous psychopathology research would account for i) the data being possibly ordinal and conflated with measurement error, ii) the plausibility of non-normal distributions in psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Reise et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Talkkari & Rosenström, 2024)</ref>, iii) that psychopathology develops continuously in time (for example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kuiper & Ryan, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ryan & Hamaker, 2022)</ref> and iv) the psychopathology process being non-stationary <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bringmann, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Schumacher et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Siepe et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, there is no study that would simultaneously consider these aspects.

Consequently, the main contributions of this article are as follows: We show formal proofs of indistinguishability conditions between SN models and CF models, without assuming stationarity or time-invariance and lending on a geometric intuition about the CF models presented in the psychometric literature (Thurstone, 1931 (Thurstone, , 1934)).
text.formatted: Consequently, the main contributions of this article are as follows: We show formal proofs of indistinguishability conditions between SN models and CF models, without assuming stationarity or time-invariance and lending on a geometric intuition about the CF models presented in the psychometric literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Thurstone, 1931</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Thurstone, , 1934))</ref>.

text.text: While we focus on distinguishability in covariance of the discrete SN models (Epskamp, 2020), we generalize to distinguishability in distribution and to continuous time models.
text.formatted: While we focus on distinguishability in covariance of the discrete SN models <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Epskamp, 2020)</ref>, we generalize to distinguishability in distribution and to continuous time models.

text.text: We also argue why the results generalise different kinds of measurement models.
Second, we produce a simple method for evaluating distinguishability between the longitudinal SN and CF models.
All of the results relate to both time series and panel modelling and so also to contemporaneous psychological methodological literature (Epskamp, 2020; Falkenström et al., 2022).
text.formatted: All of the results relate to both time series and panel modelling and so also to contemporaneous psychological methodological literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Epskamp, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Falkenström et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We begin by analytically showing conditions for indistinguishability in covariance between the longitudinal SN and CF models in a simplistic scenario, which suffices to demonstrate the main, generalisable, idea while capturing central aspects of SN and CF models.
We then continue to generalize the results.
Finally, we proceed to evaluate the consequences of the analytic results using numeric and empiric examples.
Alongside these examples, we give R scripts for evaluating the distinguishability between the longitudinal SN and CF models.
We start by reviewing a common SN model, the vector autoregressive model, and a parsimonious longitudinal CF model, with a particular focus on the covariance structure they imply over time.
Table 1 presents the main definitions and symbols used in this article to describe indistinguishability of vector autoregressive SN models and common factor models.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> presents the main definitions and symbols used in this article to describe indistinguishability of vector autoregressive SN models and common factor models.

text.text: For all analysis, we use real valued matrices.
Bold characters denote matrices and vectors.
The notation 𝐆(t) denotes a matrix, which is dependent on time 𝑡 ∈ {0, 1, … , 𝑇}.
We use similar notation for scalars, but without bolded letters.
A bold 𝟎 is used for an appropriate size matrix of zeros.
We use a subindex for time for random variables to save space.
We assume that all second moments are finite.

Most of the analytic results in the main text are based on linear algebra and covariance computation rules; some are based on known vector time series formulae (Lütkepohl, 2005; Särkkä & Solin, 2019).
text.formatted: Most of the analytic results in the main text are based on linear algebra and covariance computation rules; some are based on known vector time series formulae <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Lütkepohl, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Särkkä & Solin, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We omit proofs when they are not illustrative of the main idea, and analysis with multiple additional definitions such as the continuous time analyses, to supplementary materials and refer to them throughout the article.
We begin with a commonly applied longitudinal SN model which is the discrete time vector autoregressive model of first order (VAR(1); Epskamp, 2020; Robinaugh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We begin with a commonly applied longitudinal SN model which is the discrete time vector autoregressive model of first order (VAR(1); Epskamp, 2020; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Robinaugh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: VAR(1) represents perhaps the simplest of longitudinal SN models.
Another model suggested for application is the continuous time VAR (CT-VAR; a linear stochastic differential equation) model (Ryan & Hamaker, 2022).
text.formatted: Another model suggested for application is the continuous time VAR (CT-VAR; a linear stochastic differential equation) model <ref type="bibr">(Ryan & Hamaker, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We return to CT-VAR after discussing the main results for VAR(1) as VAR(1) works for showing the main point of this article.
Given a set of 𝐾 symptoms 𝑋 1,𝑡 , 𝑋 2,𝑡 , … , 𝑋 𝐾,𝑡 constituting a symptom process defined as the random vector 𝐗 𝑡 , the VAR(1) model is defined as where vector 𝐜 is a constant 𝐾 × 1 vector.
Here, 𝐜 is assumed zero since a constant additive term does not affect covariance.
The 𝛇 t is a 𝐾 × 1 independent "innovation" column random vector with zero expected value, 𝔼[𝛇 t ] = 0.
From the model's point of view, innovations are random effects that cause symptoms to change at every time point independently of the modelled symptom process history.
A substantive interpretation of innovations is that they represent external effects on the symptoms in the network (Hamaker et al., 2018; Jongerling et al., 2015).
text.formatted: A substantive interpretation of innovations is that they represent external effects on the symptoms in the network <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hamaker et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Jongerling et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The 𝐾 × 𝐾 innovation covariance matrix at time 𝑡 is denoted as 𝐙(𝑡) and defined as 𝔼[𝛇 𝑡 𝛇 𝑡 T ] = 𝐙(𝑡).
The 𝐾 × 𝐾 matrix 𝐀(𝑡) includes (regression) coefficients.
From the model's point of view, these coefficients are causal effects between the symptoms.
Since the VAR(1) model is first order, i.e., only the previous time point appears in (1), it is a member of a broader class of Markovian models (Klenke, 2020, pp.

Markovian models imply that next point of the process 𝐗 𝑡+1 is fully explained by the current state of 𝐗 𝑡 in the sense that there is no additional information about 𝐗 𝑡+1 in 𝐗 𝑡-1 , 𝐗 𝑡-2 , …, given that we know 𝐗 𝑡 .
Considering the models used here, a model is called Markov, if 𝐗 𝑡+1 depends directly only on 𝐗 𝑡.
For simplicity, a stationary version of VAR(1) is often used in applications (Bringmann et al., 2013 (Bringmann et al., , 2022;; Robinaugh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For simplicity, a stationary version of VAR(1) is often used in applications <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bringmann et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bringmann et al., , 2022;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Robinaugh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Stationarity implies time invariance of the coefficient matrix 𝐀(𝑡) = 𝐀, time invariance of innovation covariance 𝐙(𝑡) = 𝐙, and that 𝐀 has eigenvalues with absolute value less than one (Lütkepohl, 2005).
text.formatted: Stationarity implies time invariance of the coefficient matrix 𝐀(𝑡) = 𝐀, time invariance of innovation covariance 𝐙(𝑡) = 𝐙, and that 𝐀 has eigenvalues with absolute value less than one <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Lütkepohl, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The condition for the eigenvalues essentially ensures that covariance of the process does not grow infinitely over time and also allows for easier estimation.

However, the time invariance assumption is not aligned with the full SN theory: A hypothesis in the SN approach is that the causal effects contained in 𝐀(𝑡) would change over time as the mental disorder develops (Borsboom, 2017; Schumacher et al., 2023; van de Leemput et al., 2014).
text.formatted: However, the time invariance assumption is not aligned with the full SN theory: A hypothesis in the SN approach is that the causal effects contained in 𝐀(𝑡) would change over time as the mental disorder develops <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Schumacher et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">van de Leemput et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we relax stationarity restrictions on 𝐀(𝑡) for our analysis.
Similarly, we allow time dependence of 𝐙(𝑡), as the innovation covariance might change over time as well (Bringmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, we allow time dependence of 𝐙(𝑡), as the innovation covariance might change over time as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bringmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A longitudinal SN model can be extended to include a measurement model, which will be discussed in a separate section after presenting the CF model.
For our purposes, we are interested in the cross-covariance of the symptom process 𝐗 𝑡 .
When we discuss cross-covariance, we implicitly mean the cross-covariance of 𝐗 𝑡 unless otherwise stated.
Cross-covariance describes between time point covariance as shown soon.
We denote with Δ𝑡 ∈ {0,1,2, … } an increment in time.
We first define 𝐏(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) ≔ { ∏ 𝐀(𝑡 + 𝑘) Δ𝑡-1 𝑘=0 , Δ𝑡 > 0 𝐈, otherwise.
text.formatted: We first define 𝐏(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) ≔ { ∏ 𝐀(𝑡 + 𝑘) Δ𝑡-1 𝑘=0 , Δ𝑡 > 0 𝐈, otherwise.

text.text: This can be called the transition matrix from t to 𝑡 + Δ𝑡 (Särkkä & Solin, 2019), where 𝐈 is an identity matrix.
text.formatted: This can be called the transition matrix from t to 𝑡 + Δ𝑡 <ref type="bibr">(Särkkä & Solin, 2019)</ref>, where 𝐈 is an identity matrix.

text.text: The cross-covariance 𝔼[𝐗 𝑡+Δ𝑡 𝐗 𝑡 T ] of a VAR(1) model for Δ𝑡 > 0 is (note that 𝐏(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) = 𝐀 Δ𝑡 in the stationary case 𝐀(𝑡) = 𝐀).
text.formatted: The cross-covariance 𝔼[𝐗 𝑡+Δ𝑡 𝐗 𝑡 T ] of a VAR(1) model for Δ𝑡 > 0 is (note that 𝐏(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) = 𝐀 Δ𝑡 in the stationary case 𝐀(𝑡) = 𝐀).

text.text: We still need to obtain the within time point covariance 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡), which is the cross-covariance with Δ𝑡 = 0.
Unlike in the stationary case, we cannot in general analytically solve for 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡).
Given 𝐀(𝑡) and 𝐙(𝑡), we still need some 𝑡 for which we know 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡), so that we can compute 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑠), 𝑠 ≠ 𝑡, for other time points using 𝐀(𝑡) and 𝐙(𝑡).
Hence, for our purposes, we assume that the within time point covariance is known at some time point 𝑡, if not stated otherwise.

This assumption defines 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡 + Δ𝑡) iteratively at subsequent time points as well, because 𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡 + 1) = Cov (𝐀(𝑡)𝐗 𝑡 + 𝛇 𝑡+1 ⏟ =𝐗 𝑡+1 , 𝐀(𝑡)𝐗 𝑡 + 𝛇 𝑡+1 ⏟ =𝐗 𝑡+1 ) = 𝐀(𝑡)𝚺 VAR(1) (𝑡)𝐀(𝑡) T + 𝐙(𝑡 + 1).
Supplementary Material 1 presents additional details on VAR(1) cross-covariance computations.
CF models present the symptoms as effects of a latent disease or liability, which is the CF itself.
In other words, contrary to SN models, there are no direct associations between the symptoms (Cramer et al., 2010).
text.formatted: In other words, contrary to SN models, there are no direct associations between the symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Cramer et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A common longitudinal CF model is a one-dimensional CF model, where the effects of the CF, called the factor loadings, do not change over time, that is 𝚲(𝑡) = 𝚲 (Liu et al., 2017; Widaman et al., 2010).
text.formatted: A common longitudinal CF model is a one-dimensional CF model, where the effects of the CF, called the factor loadings, do not change over time, that is 𝚲(𝑡) = 𝚲 <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Liu et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Widaman et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: We consider this model first as it gives an illustrative and substantively important special case and then generalize to time-varying loadings.
Further, we introduce a measurement model for observations 𝐘 𝑡 , which is discussed more thoroughly after CF model presentation.
We denote the CF itself by a random variable 𝜂 𝑡 .

Emphasizing that we focus on the symptom process 𝐗 𝑡 , the CF model of observed data 𝐘 𝑡 is where 𝚲 is a 𝐾 × 1 column vector of factor loadings and the 𝐾 × 1 vector 𝛜 𝑡 is measurement error or residual (see below).
Similarly to the case of VAR(1), we assume 𝔼[𝜂 𝑡 ] = 0 without loss of generality meaning that 𝔼[𝐗 𝑡 ] = 0.
The cross-covariance, for all Δ𝑡, of 𝐗 𝑡 is 𝐊 CF (𝑡 + Δ𝑡, t) = 𝜓(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡)𝚲𝚲 T , ( where 𝜓(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) = Cov(𝜂 𝑡+Δ𝑡 , 𝜂 𝑡 ) is the cross-covariance of the CF (See Supplementary Material 2).
A special case is where the CF is an autoregressive process, so that where 𝜁 𝜂 𝑡 is an innovation for the CF and 𝜙(𝑡 -1) is an autoregression coefficient.
This is an interesting case with respect to the distinguishability of the SN and CF models presented here, specifically due to it being a Markov model.
When the CF itself is modelled as in (7), we will call the CF model for the symptom process 𝐗 𝑡 a Markov CF model to ease readability of the results to follow.
For more cross-covariance computations relevant to this article, see Supplementary Material 2.
In application, the symptom process 𝐗 𝑡 is not observed directly, and so there is a need to include a measurement model that maps the symptoms to the observations 𝐘 𝑡 .

Both, the CF and the SN models can be extended to observations via a measurement model with additive and uncorrelated or correlated errors (Epskamp, 2020; McArdle, 2009; Rhemtulla et al., 2020; Schuurman et al., 2015; Schuurman & Hamaker, 2019; Vogelsmeier et al., 2019; Widaman et al., 2010).

text.text: We clarify the meaning of correlated errors 𝛜 𝑡 of 𝐘 𝑡 and why we can focus our analysis on 𝐗 𝑡.
In many cases, a serially correlated residual structure is considered.
For example, Molenaar (1985) discerns the 'aetiological process' from the orthogonal 'residual'.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Molenaar (1985)</ref> discerns the 'aetiological process' from the orthogonal 'residual'.

text.text: On one hand, it has been argued that correlated residuals are justified as there might be contextual or methodological reasons for associations unique to some indicator due to wording and response format specific to the indicator (Cole et al., 2007; Hoyle, 2023).

text.text: On the other hand, it has been suggested that residuals to a CF could be a SN (Epskamp, Rhemtulla, et al., 2017).

text.text: To avoid ambiguity, we simply consider the residual to represent measurement artefact unrelated to the symptom process.
To obtain a like-for-like comparison, we analyse the cross-covariance of the symptom process 𝐗 𝑡 .

This is justifiable as, for example, the within time point covariance structure of additive measurement errors is Cov(𝐘 𝑡 , 𝐘 𝑡 ) = Cov(𝐗 𝑡 + 𝛜 𝑡 , 𝐗 𝑡 + 𝛜 𝑡 ) = Cov(𝐗 𝑡 , 𝐗 𝑡 ) + Cov(𝛜 𝑡 , 𝛜 𝑡 ), and (by independence) for Δ𝑡 > 0 the cross-covariance is 𝔼[𝐘 𝑡+Δ𝑡 𝐘 t T ] = 𝔼[(𝐗 𝑡+Δ𝑡 + 𝛜 𝑡+Δ𝑡 )(𝐗 𝑡 + 𝛜 𝑡 ) T ] = 𝐊(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) + 𝔼[𝛜 𝑡+Δ𝑡 𝛜 𝑡 T ], meaning that we can separate cross-covariance analysis of 𝐗 𝑡 from 𝛜 𝑡 .

text.text: Thus, given the same measurement model for a SN and a CF model, it suffices to show indistinguishability in terms of 𝐗 𝑡.
This holds also for a more general measurement model.
We define a measurement model by a measurement function 𝑚 that maps 𝐗 𝑡 to observations 𝐘 𝑡 .

text.text: In below, we will generalise to indistinguishability in distribution.

When indistinguishability in distribution holds, the distribution of 𝐗 𝑡 is the same under both models and so is the distribution of 𝑚(𝐗 𝑡 ) under a measurement function 𝑚 defined on ℝ 𝐾. 4 Further, in application, we are interested in what kind of distribution or covariance an estimated model implies for 𝐗 𝑡 .

text.text: That is, after fitting a model for the symptom process, accompanied by some measurement model, we consider the measurement model as nuisance and focus on the symptom process.
Another natural extension is to a multilevel (hierarchical) model, in which each subject's time series is treated as a draw from a population of time series.
In this case, we would allow the parameters to vary between-subjects; e.g., we might allow the coefficient matrix of VAR(1) model 𝐀 𝑖 (𝑡) to depend on subject 𝑖.
For 𝑁 subjects, this produces 𝑁 VAR(1) models which might, or might not, be indistinguishable from a CF model.
Another multilevel structure is the random-intercept used in the SN literature (Epskamp, 2020) and CF literature (Widaman et al., 2010), wherein we allow the constant 𝐜 to depend on subject.
text.formatted: Another multilevel structure is the random-intercept used in the SN literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Epskamp, 2020)</ref> and CF literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Widaman et al., 2010)</ref>, wherein we allow the constant 𝐜 to depend on subject.

text.text: In the empirical application below, we use a graded response model accompanied by random-intercept structure.
We can now present conditions for indistinguishability of the two symptom process models.
We use the VAR(1) and one CF model to show the main idea and then generalise.
First, note that the VAR(1) imposes the Markov property, because the symptoms 𝐗 𝑡 only depend on 𝐗 𝑡-1 .

Second, the CF model factor loadings 𝚲 defines a vector space in which 𝐗 𝑡 varies (M. L. Eaton, 2007). 5For a one CF model this space is the direction of 𝚲, which is a one-dimensional space embedded to the 𝐾-dimensional symptom space.
text.formatted: Second, the CF model factor loadings 𝚲 defines a vector space in which 𝐗 𝑡 varies (M. L. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Eaton, 2007)</ref>. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">5</ref>For a one CF model this space is the direction of 𝚲, which is a one-dimensional space embedded to the 𝐾-dimensional symptom space.

text.text: Thus, two hypotheses are obtained for indistinguishability between a one CF model and a VAR(1) model:
Hypothesis 1: The CF model must equal a Markov CF model in (cross-)covariance.
Hypothesis 2: The 𝐗 𝑡 must stay in the direction of 𝚲 for both models.
We begin by stating two indistinguishability conditions (IC) that we then show to be necessary and sufficient for indistinguishability.
These conditions together are then shown to imply that both hypotheses are true.
IC 1: The vector of factor loadings 𝚲 must be an eigenvector of 𝐀(𝑡), with eigenvalue 𝜓(𝑡 + 1, 𝑡)/𝜓(𝑡, 𝑡).
IC 2: VAR(1) innovation covariance 𝐙(𝑡) must equal Var(𝜁 𝜂 𝑡 )𝚲𝚲 T.
(IC 1 is proven in Supplementary Material 3 and IC 2 in Supplementary Material 4.)
With IC 1 and IC 2, we have a complete description for model indistinguishability: All parameters relevant to cross-covariance are constrained by IC 1 and IC 2.
Since IC 1 was a consequence of assuming model indistinguishability, it is necessary.
Further, IC 2 is a consequence of the necessary IC 1 (and model indistinguishability), and so it is also necessary.
We will denote a coefficient matrix satisfying IC 1 as 𝐀 ̃(𝑡) and, similarly, innovation covariance satisfying IC 2 as 𝐙 ̃(𝑡).
Main Result 1: Indistinguishability Conditions 1 and 2 are necessary and sufficient for indistinguishability.
(Main Result 1, especially sufficiency, is proven in Supplementary Material 5.)

To see why Hypothesis 1 is true, first note that 𝜓(𝑡 + 1, 𝑡)/𝜓(𝑡, 𝑡) is the formula for the autoregression coefficient 𝜙(𝑡) in a Markov CF model shown in (7), as it equals a regression coefficient in a simple regression.

Further, it can be shown that IC 1 implies a cross-covariance for Δ𝑡 > 0, which is indistinguishable from a Markov CF model (Supplementary Material 4, Lemma 1): where 𝐏 ̃(𝑡 + Δ𝑡, 𝑡) is (2) with 𝐀(t + k) = 𝐀 ̃(𝑡 + 𝑘) satisfying IC 1.

text.text: Second, IC 2 implies that the within time point covariance must be indistinguishable from a Markov CF model as well.

Therefore, Hypothesis 1 is true.
Next, we show why Hypothesis 2 is true, meaning that the symptom process is in the direction defined by 𝚲.
First, intuitively, if 𝐗 𝑡 is not in the direction defined by 𝚲, then the CF model cannot explain variations in the symptom process perfectly.
So, suppose 𝐗 𝑡 is in this direction.
Then 𝐗 𝑡 = 𝚲𝛼, for some value 𝛼 ∈ ℝ that defines the coordinate of 𝐗 𝑡 .

text.text: Therefore, the space defined by columns of 𝐙 ̃(𝑡) is the same as the space defined by columns of 𝚲.
Consequently, 𝐗 𝑡 , 𝐀 ̃(𝑡)𝐗 𝑡 and 𝛇 𝑡 must all lie in the direction of 𝚲 by IC 1 and 2, informally proving Hypothesis 2.
In fact, Hypothesis 2 holds to more generality when we allow the factor loadings to vary over time, and we allow there to be multiple CFs.
Notably, the generality is not limited to i) indistinguishability in covariance, ii) Markov models nor iii) a one CF model.
We will see that, when Hypothesis 2 holds, there exists a distributionally indistinguishable CF model for a more general class of SN models than VAR(1).
Hypothesis 1 also generalises to non-Markov models.
To present the results, we introduce a new model, S-VAR(c), which can be understood as a SN model with lagged effects up to 𝑐 lags and instantaneous (lag 0) effects.
In SN literature, conceptually similar modelling choices to S-VAR(c) has been discussed (Epskamp, 2020).

A similar CF model is obtained by modelling 𝛈 𝑡 as an S-VAR(c) (Bai & Wang, 2015).

text.text: Further, a multidimensional CF model generalises to a vector of 𝑞 CFs 𝛈 𝑡 with a 𝐾 × 𝑞 factor loadings matrix 𝚲(𝑡), such that 𝐗 𝑡 = 𝚲(𝑡)𝛈 𝑡.
We state the result in two parts as follows.
Let 𝒯 be an arbitrary time index set of non-negative real numbers.
Then we have:

Main Result 2, part 1: If, and only if, a symptom network model implies that 𝐗 𝑡 ∈ span 𝚲(𝑡) almost surely, for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝒯, for some matrix 𝚲(𝑡) ∈ ℝ 𝐾×𝑞 with linearly independent columns and 𝑞 < 𝐾, then there exists a CF model indistinguishable in distribution.
text.formatted: Main Result 2, part 1: If, and only if, a symptom network model implies that 𝐗 𝑡 ∈ span 𝚲(𝑡) almost surely, for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝒯, for some matrix 𝚲(𝑡) ∈ ℝ 𝐾×𝑞 with linearly independent columns and 𝑞 < 𝐾, then there exists a CF model indistinguishable in distribution.

text.text: (Main Result 2 is proven in Supplementary Material 6.)
Thus, the idea from Hypothesis 2 generalises.
We highlight two aspects that are generally important.

First, it turns out that the indistinguishability in distribution is an implication of indistinguishability in covariance: When a CF model indistinguishable in covariance exists, a CF model indistinguishable in distribution exists as well.
This makes it interesting to analyse the (cross-)covariance of SN models, as we will do below, to see if some distributionally indistinguishable CF model could explain observed data.
Second, we also obtain a potentially useful result about mean indistinguishability.
Applying Main Result 2 to the random vector 𝐗 𝑡 + 𝐜 we notice that the mean shift by a 𝐾 × 1 constant vector 𝐜 must be in the space defined by 𝚲(𝑡).

This is because 𝔼[𝐗 𝑡 + 𝐜] = 𝐜 and so, if the constant vector is not within that space, then Main Result 2 cannot hold; 𝐗 𝑡 + 𝐜 would have to lie outside the space defined by 𝚲(𝑡) with non-zero probability, for the expectation to not lie in that space.
We now generalize the result to continuous time (CT) models, which have been suggested as an alternative to discrete time SN models (Ryan & Hamaker, 2022).
text.formatted: We now generalize the result to continuous time (CT) models, which have been suggested as an alternative to discrete time SN models <ref type="bibr">(Ryan & Hamaker, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, Main Result (part 1) holds when we allow time to be non-discrete, and a CT CF model can be built from a CT vector autoregressive (CT-VAR) model (multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck; Oravecz et al., 2009 Oravecz et al., , 2016)).
text.formatted: Specifically, Main Result (part 1) holds when we allow time to be non-discrete, and a CT CF model can be built from a CT vector autoregressive (CT-VAR) model (multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck; <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Oravecz et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Oravecz et al., , 2016))</ref>.

text.text: A CT-VAR model is a linear stochastic differential equation The change in symptoms 𝑑𝐗 𝑡 is modelled as a deterministic function of the current state weighted by the coefficient matrix 𝐀(𝑡).
Randomness is induced by a Brownian motion 𝐁 𝑡 , which can become correlated via 𝐋(𝑡).
The 𝑑𝑡 and 𝑑𝐁 𝑡 are notation for small increments in time and the Brownian motion process.
We can conceive a CT CF model by replacing 𝐗 𝑡 with 𝛈 𝑡 and relating the symptoms to the CF via factor loadings in the expected manner.
Since continuous time models require multiple additional definitions and technical details unimportant to the main point of this article these details are omitted to Supplementary Material 6.
We highlight an important point about the CT and discrete VAR models: The CT-VAR model is relatable to a VAR(1).
Both are Markovian and we can discretize a CT-VAR model to a VAR(1) model that is indistinguishable in distribution.
Nevertheless, we state the result as follows.
Let 𝒯 be a time index set of non-negative real numbers.
Then we have: Main Result 3: A CT-VAR model is indistinguishable in distribution from a CT CF model if, and only if, 𝐗 𝑡 lies in span 𝚲(𝑡) almost surely, for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝒯.
Under a mild additional regularity condition, the respective CT-VAR model can be transformed to a pathwise indistinguishable CT CF model.
(Main result 3 is proven in Supplementary Material 6.)
To summarize, longitudinal CF models can be transformed to SN models.
For the reverse relationship, the main condition is that the SN model implies symptom process must lie in some space understood as the space defined by the factor loadings.
To see if a SN model is indistinguishable in distribution from a CF model, it suffices to show that it is indistinguishable in covariance from a CF model.
When a Markov SN model is indistinguishable from some CF model, the same SN model is indistinguishable from a Markov CF model.
The same applies for S-VAR(c) SN models; when such a model is indistinguishable from some CF model, there exists a distributionally indistinguishable CF model with an S-VAR(c) CF process.
For CT-VAR models, the same main condition applies.
CT models can be either discretized to VAR(1) models or transformed directly.
We make two final notes before the numerical and empirical examples.
First, we note that under model indistinguishability the VAR(1) model, S-VAR(c) and CT-VAR are not identified.
This is because there are excess dimensions in the model.
In other words, there is multicollinearity due to all 𝐾 symptoms being parametrizable as linear transformations of 𝑞 < 𝐾 CFs.
text.formatted: In other words, there is multicollinearity due to all 𝐾 symptoms being parametrizable as linear transformations of 𝑞 < 𝐾 CFs.

text.text: This can cause spurious results to occur when the model is near indistinguishable as we will show.

Second, whilst multicollinearity is a consequence of indistinguishability, part of the substantive discussion is tied to how factor loadings change, or do not, over time (Fried et al., 2016; Widaman et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Second, whilst multicollinearity is a consequence of indistinguishability, part of the substantive discussion is tied to how factor loadings change, or do not, over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Fried et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Widaman et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Loadings that vary abruptly over time might not make sense from a substantive viewpoint, as they make the CF hard to interpret.
Therefore, while we generalised the results to arbitrarily changing factor loadings, the time-invariant case might be the most interesting one.
We return to our original focus on the time-invariant case in the next section.
We can now focus on exploring the results of analytic section with examples.
To begin with, consider Figure 2.
text.formatted: To begin with, consider Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>.

text.text: It has four coefficient matrices.
They were generated by simulating data from a one CF model and fitting a VAR(1) model to the simulated data.
We recall that a CF model implied cross-covariance is not sufficient for identifying a VAR(1) model: There are many indistinguishable VAR(1) models for their respective indistinguishable CF model.
Thus, we added independent normally distributed white noise, with a negligible variance of 0.01, to the simulated data entries.
That is, we made all of the fitted VAR(1) models identifiable, yet, nearly indistinguishable from a CF model, with which the data was simulated.
All VAR(1) model coefficients ended up suggesting sometimes opposite directions of association (negative vs.
positive).

Given that the etiological interpretation of a CF model is considerably distinct from these randomly identified coefficient matrices, this should be motivation enough for us to find a way to quantify distinguishability from a CF model in empirical applications.
To proceed, first, we show how cross-covariance matrices can be evaluated for a more thorough analysis of a stationary VAR(1) model.
Second, the steps shown in the first part are applied in an empirical example.
We conclude by giving quick-to-use functions to conduct the distinguishability analyses in applied research.
The main points of the analysis are discussed here, while Supplementary Material 7 provides additional details about technical aspects especially.
For the graphical illustrations of SN models we use the R -package 'qgraph' (Epskamp et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For the graphical illustrations of SN models we use the R -package 'qgraph' <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Epskamp et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, this particular way the SNs are visualized has been promoted as a strength of the SN approach (Bringmann, 2024).
text.formatted: Specifically, this particular way the SNs are visualized has been promoted as a strength of the SN approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bringmann, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We first show how distinguishability can be summarized using the eigenvalues (or singular values, discussed below) and eigenvectors of the cross-covariance matrices implied by a VAR(1) model (hereafter cross-covariance, in short).
The first step resembles, but is distinct to, what is done in the scree plot method (Cattell, 1966).
text.formatted: The first step resembles, but is distinct to, what is done in the scree plot method <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cattell, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: The intuition is that, if a (one) CF model is true, then we should see a "dominant" component in cross-covariance matrices, indicated by the first eigenvalue remaining large over time increments: 𝐊(𝑡, 𝑡), 𝐊(𝑡 + 1, 𝑡), 𝐊(𝑡 + 2, 𝑡) … 𝐊(𝑇, 𝑡), where 𝑇 is the last time point.
The scree plot method is analogous to this, but it is based solely on the within time point covariance, 𝐊(𝑡, 𝑡) matrix.

If the cross-covariance is perfectly explained by a CF (Markov, or other), there is only one component and so the first eigenvalue is the only nonzero eigenvalue, which can be ascertained from the IC 1 and IC 2. 7 That is, a one CF model implies rank one (cross-)covariance.
text.formatted: If the cross-covariance is perfectly explained by a CF (Markov, or other), there is only one component and so the first eigenvalue is the only nonzero eigenvalue, which can be ascertained from the IC 1 and IC 2. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">7</ref> That is, a one CF model implies rank one (cross-)covariance.

text.text: If the first eigenvalue is not stably large, additional components may be required to explain the cross-covariance.
Suppose that we see a dominant component in the cross-covariance, and interpret it as a CF.
We do not yet know anything about the factor loadings.
We need to analyze if the VAR(1) model produces a stable direction, which could be interpreted as the direction of the factor loadings.
Consequently, we then inspect if the first eigenvector of cross-covariance retains its direction over time increments.
If it does, then the largest component has a stable direction over time.
If there is no stable direction, the largest component can lose its meaning as representing a consistently interpretable CF.

More precisely, we do this by computing the congruency coefficientfoot_6  (Reise et al., 2000) between the first eigenvectors of subsequent cross-covariance matrices, (𝐊(𝑡 + 1, 𝑡), 𝐊(𝑡 + 2, 𝑡 + 1)), … , (𝐊(𝑇 -1, 𝑇 -2), 𝐊(𝑇, 𝑇 -1)) up to some 𝑇.
text.formatted: More precisely, we do this by computing the congruency coefficient<ref type="foot" target="#foot_6">foot_6</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Reise et al., 2000)</ref> between the first eigenvectors of subsequent cross-covariance matrices, (𝐊(𝑡 + 1, 𝑡), 𝐊(𝑡 + 2, 𝑡 + 1)), … , (𝐊(𝑇 -1, 𝑇 -2), 𝐊(𝑇, 𝑇 -1)) up to some 𝑇.

text.text: Essentially, if the congruency coefficient is always exactly 1, the factor loadings would be perfectly time-invariant.
If the congruency coefficient is not stably large, e.g., consistently larger than 0.90 (Hurley & Cattell, 1962; Reise et al., 2000; Somma et al., 2019), then the loadings are not time-invariant.
text.formatted: If the congruency coefficient is not stably large, e.g., consistently larger than 0.90 <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Hurley & Cattell, 1962;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Reise et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Somma et al., 2019)</ref>, then the loadings are not time-invariant.

text.text: We use the absolute value of the congruency, as the CF direction and the eigenvectors are unidentified up to sign.

It is worth noting that we use the base R function eigen, which orders eigenvalues in terms of their modulus (absolute value) so that ties are solved by selecting the value with positive weight for the imaginary part first and for ties between real valued eigenvalues the positive eigenvalues come first.
How to select 𝑇 depends on the substantive context and data used.
For example, analyses with daily measurements over a few weeks might consider it feasible to include 𝑇 up to the data horizon of few weeks.

Alternatively, one might consider 𝑇 up to when all components are near zero so that little variation is left to analyse. 9 This might, however, require computing the crosscovariance well past what is a realistic time horizon for the estimated model.
text.formatted: Alternatively, one might consider 𝑇 up to when all components are near zero so that little variation is left to analyse. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_7">9</ref> This might, however, require computing the crosscovariance well past what is a realistic time horizon for the estimated model.

text.text: Although we focus here on seeing if there is a single dominant component, we show in Supplementary Material 7 that the choice of 𝑇 can be consequential especially for models where multiple relevant components exist.
In addition, while intuitive for professionals familiar with factor analysis, eigenvalues are more complex for analysis of cross-covariance.
Cross-covariance matrices can have negative eigenvalues with imaginary parts.
A simpler solution is to use singular values.
Singular values, obtained from the singular value decomposition of the cross-covariance, are always non-negative and real valued.
They have two important properties.
First, for the within time point covariance 𝚺(𝑡), singular values equal eigenvalues.
This means that the 'total variance', which is the sum of the eigenvalues of 𝚺(𝑡), is also the sum of the singular values.
For cross-covariance matrices, the sum of the singular values is understood as maximal total cross-covariance under arbitrary rotation (Schönemann, 1966).
text.formatted: For cross-covariance matrices, the sum of the singular values is understood as maximal total cross-covariance under arbitrary rotation <ref type="bibr">(Schönemann, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Intuitively, the sum is maximal cross-covariance when we are naïve to factor loading direction(s).
This defines meaning of the value 𝜎 𝑗 / ∑ 𝜎 𝑗 𝐾 𝑗=1 as the proportion of maximal total cross-covariance explained by the j-th singular value.

Second, Before showing examples, we summarise with a non-exhaustive list of different scenarios and possible interpretations is: i) If there is a dominant component, and it has a stable direction (both are true), then there is evidence that a CF, with time invariant factor loadings, is (informally put) contained in the VAR(1) model.

ii) If there is a dominant component, but it does not have a stable direction, then the interpretation of this component can be questionable, though in principle would not contradict there being a CF with time-varying factor loadings.
iii) If no dominant component is seen, then there is no support for a CF, at least if we require the CF to be the largest cause of the symptoms.
This is independent of the stability of the (first) eigenvector(s).
iv) If a relatively large component is seen, with a stable direction, but also other nonnegligible components appear, the result is inconclusive.
Argumentation can be continued using other observations or reasoning.
v) When there are multiple components that are comparable in size, the congruency for the largest direction is insufficient for a clear view about if a CF -like component exists.
We give numeric examples and additional details how to analyse the congruencies in these scenarios in Supplementary Material 7.

To conduct a complete analysis of whether a (one) CF model could be rejected in empirical data, we used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data freely available from the supplementary materials of Fried et al. (2022).
text.formatted: To conduct a complete analysis of whether a (one) CF model could be rejected in empirical data, we used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data freely available from the supplementary materials of <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Fried et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: The data included 79 subjects.
For each subject, a two-week period was sampled.
Each day, four assessments were taken.

Three subjects were not included due to having less than 50 total assessments (distinctively fewer than all other subjects), and one subject was not included due to subsequent missing values over a week.
All observed variables were truncated to four categories, instead of five, due to low cell counts in the last category.
For a more detailed view of the data, we refer to Fried et al. (2022).
text.formatted: For a more detailed view of the data, we refer to <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Fried et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: In two separate analyses, with two distinct data sets, a latent VAR(1) model was estimated.
While the models were estimated by including a measurement model, as well as time-of-day effects and multilevel structure (see below), the results themselves solely relate to the latent VAR(1).
This VAR(1) model was analysed for indistinguishability using the methods constructed above.
Hence, the results rely on the assumption that the latent VAR(1) model is estimated correctly.
We lay out how we estimated the model: The model was specified as a Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) model and implemented in the cmdstanr package (Gabry et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We lay out how we estimated the model: The model was specified as a Stan <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpenter et al., 2017)</ref> model and implemented in the cmdstanr package <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Gabry et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimation was run with 4 chains, 4000 iterations per chain.
In both analyses discussed below, the chains converged well, and no signs of divergent paths were seen.
The model has the following important assumptions and properties.
First, the symptoms must behave as a process with the Markov property.
Second, to reflect our prior belief, we set a weak prior distribution for the innovation and coefficient matrices, which is centred around a VAR(1) indistinguishable from a CF model.
Third, for the observed ordinal variables, a probit measurement model was used (e.g., Samejima, 2010; see measurement model section above).
text.formatted: Third, for the observed ordinal variables, a probit measurement model was used (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Samejima, 2010</ref>; see measurement model section above).

text.text: Fourth, missingness in the data was handled by including unobserved responses in the data as parameters in the model.
Fifth, multilevel structure was accounted for by allowing individuals to have their own subject-specific intercept terms.
Sixth, no detrending was done.
Seventh, we also included a time-of-day variable (morning, midday, noon, evening) as a covariate to model systematic daily changes in the symptoms.
This variable was allowed to affect each symptom differently.
A sensitivity analysis was conducted with prior parameterisation that does not favour a CF model.

The full Stan model specifications can be found online (https://osf.io/hu7g9/files/osfstorage?view_only=184ae735527d4616ae96af5c0201e1c8 ) and the mathematical definitions in Supplementary Material 8.

text.text: In the first analysis, we restricted the observed variables to a set, which would plausibly be from an "anxiety liability" CF (difficulties in relaxing, worry, nervousness; see Fried et al., 2022).

text.text: In Figure 4, the absolute values of eigenvalues and congruency coefficients are shown for the posterior mean VAR(1) model.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4</ref>, the absolute values of eigenvalues and congruency coefficients are shown for the posterior mean VAR(1) model.

text.text: The analysis suggests that a single component dominates the cross-covariance matrices over time-increments, and it has a stable direction.
For all posterior draws, the first singular value explained a larger proportion than 0.90 over all latent VAR(1) implied cross-covariance.
Similarly, for all posterior draws, all the congruency coefficients between subsequent first eigenvectors were larger than 0.90.
Taken together, there is strong support for interpreting the estimated VAR(1) as a CF model.

We then repeated the analysis for a larger set of observed variables (difficulties in relaxing, worry, nervousness, and, in addition, tiredness, hunger, feeling alone, feeling angry; Fried et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We then repeated the analysis for a larger set of observed variables (difficulties in relaxing, worry, nervousness, and, in addition, tiredness, hunger, feeling alone, feeling angry; <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Fried et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Since this set contains more variables, and arguably variables not relatable to anxiety liability alone, it is less likely to produce a VAR(1) model that would behave as a Markov CF model.
Indeed, as seen in Figure 5, though the first component is distinctively large, two more non-zero components appear through the cross-covariance matrices over time increments.
text.formatted: Indeed, as seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">5</ref>, though the first component is distinctively large, two more non-zero components appear through the cross-covariance matrices over time increments.

text.text: For all the posterior draws, the first singular value never explained more than 0.90 over all latent VAR(1) implied cross-covariance.
However, for all the posterior draws, the congruency coefficients between subsequent first eigenvectors were larger than 0.90.
Also note that feelings of hunger and tiredness were largely explained by time of day, hence the lower innovation covariance.

Especially since the analysis was done with the prior belief that the VAR(1) would be indistinguishable, which was explicitly stated with prior distributions for the parameters, we conclude that a single CF is not sufficient to explain the cross-covariance implied by this model.
Yet it would be an overstatement to completely reject a CF being involved, especially since the first component is distinctively large and has a stable direction.
Sensitivity analyses with another prior parameterisation not favouring the CF model led to the same conclusion for both the first and the second analysis.
The sensitivity analyses, and plots with time increments up to 50, are found in Supplementary Material 8, sensitivity analyses -section.
Using the cross-covariances implied by an estimated stationary VAR(1) SN model, we can assess its properties via decomposing the cross-covariance.
This is similar to a scree plot but generalized to cross-covariance (not just within time point covariance) and is based on an estimated model, while the scree plot uses empirical covariance.

Since we are using model implied cross-covariance(s), we have the possibility to use an explicit measurement model for the ordinal items, to account for multilevel structures and other variables alongside other possibilities.
The downside of this is that this approach relies on a correctly specified model and an identifiable estimation scheme.
We used a heuristic reference of 0.90 for the first singular value divided by the sum of all singular values, and 0.90 for congruency.

However, historically cut-off values suggested (and simultaneously criticized) by methodologists have caused problems in progression of research (Hayduk et al., 2007; Hu & Bentler, 1999; Lakens, 2021; McNeish & Wolf, 2023; Xia & Yang, 2019).

A strength of psychometric models in psychopathology research is that we can formally analyze their theoretical predictions to guide empirical research, theory development, and, eventually, improve mental health interventions (Bringmann et al., 2022; Krueger & Eaton, 2015; Ryan & Hamaker, 2022).

text.text: Building upon formal analysis, we made two separate contributions to this field of research.
First, we mathematically, numerically, and empirically showed that longitudinal CF models with the Markov property can be related to a SN model that is indistinguishable in distribution.
Further, we demonstrated how to use this fact in practice.

As longitudinal and time series data and analyses are becoming more prevalent (Bringmann, 2024; Robinaugh et al.,    13 The analysis ran for 270 ms on a single core of Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 7 165H, 1400 Mhz.
2020), the results carry particular significance: They underscore the importance of carefully evaluating the (in)distinguishability between the fitted SN and CF models.
Since a large class of longitudinal CF models can be presented as SN models, there is not always a need to perform completely separate analyses for comparisons.

Given the overlap, it suffices to derive the implied cross-covariance from one model, such as a VAR(1) (or continuous time VAR) model, and analyze to what extent this cross-covariance is incompatible with a CF model.
This can shorten analysis, especially when the research aim is not focused on theoretical comparison.
The methods provided above offer a quick solution to check this assumption, as they only require the user to input a stationary VAR(1) model.
This adds to known possibilities (Schumacher et al., 2024) on how to improve applied SN analysis.
text.formatted: This adds to known possibilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Schumacher et al., 2024)</ref> on how to improve applied SN analysis.

text.text: If a CF model seems plausible, more rigorous testing and model comparisons can be done.
Nuanced approaches, with case-by-case consideration of substantive theory, are likely needed when no clear distinction is seen.

We mention some further applied models and data structures for which our analytic results are applicable: First, the analytic results generalize to latent VAR(1) SN models in addition to observed ones.

That is, our results and tools are applicable also in the possible future of SN analyses where measurement models for SNs are included (Bringmann et al., 2022; Epskamp, Rhemtulla, et al., 2017; Schumacher et al., 2024).
text.formatted: That is, our results and tools are applicable also in the possible future of SN analyses where measurement models for SNs are included <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bringmann et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Epskamp, Rhemtulla, et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Schumacher et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, though the analytic results were shown from a 𝑁 = 1 perspective, they generalize to multilevel models with multiple subjects (as was done in the 4.3 Empirical application -section).

The same linear algebra and statistics apply for the coefficient and innovation covariance matrices, independent of the level of analysis -as long as there is a VAR(1) ingrained in a model 14 that one is willing to interpret, then using methods given here is feasible.
For a CT-VAR model, discretization can be a pragmatic choice for stationary models, as shown in Supplementary Material 6.
Finally, even if studying distinguishability would not be of interest, analysis of cross-covariance matrices can still show how the symptoms behave over time in a SN.
E.g., informally put, we could analyze to what extent the SN is oriented around a certain direction(s) (component(s)).
Methods given here can be useful for this purpose as well.
The models presented here could be extended in various directions, and reanalyzed if necessary.

For example, assumptions driven by theory, or a specific hypothesis about what kind of changes over time are expected for a SN, such as critical transitions (van de Leemput et al., 2014) or a trait-like time independent CF (Cole, 2012; Hoffart & Johnson, 2020), will likely improve distinguishability.

text.text: Second, the methods given here are meant to give a minimal check for disputing a CF model.
Using them does not mean that more rigorous analyses would not be ultimately needed as research progresses.
Third, analysis of eigenvalues and singular values and -vectors of cross-covariance matrices does not have a fixed theorydriven "cut-off" against which one would base decisions.
We tested an approximation created for the root mean squared error of approximation (RMSEA), which is grounded in statistical literature of structural equation models.
Due to the non-invertibility of low rank implied crosscovariances, a singularity is encountered in the discrepancy function required for computing RMSEA accurately.
Thus, simulation-based methods were tested, but they were not stable enough for reliable use.
These experimental methods are given in the open science framework project, alongside the methods suggested for use.
Estimated SN models that seemingly have a complex structure can be indistinguishable from a common factor model.
Though this is a problem, it simultaneously leads to easily applicable methods for quantifying between-theory differences, which in turn aid theory development in the long run.
We suggest using the methods provided here as a minimal check before coefficients of stationary longitudinal SN models are interpreted, and also when interested in comparing CF and SN theories.

Remark 1: Indistinguishability in within time point covariance and in distribution coincide.
We note that the proof of the contrapositive shows that indistinguishability in within time point covariance is necessary for showing that there exists a CF model indistinguishable in distribution.

The sufficient condition 𝐗 𝑡 ∈ span 𝚲 ̃(𝑡), on the other hand, implies that the within time point covariance admits a form 𝚺(𝑡) = 𝚲 ̃(t)𝚺 𝛈 (𝑡)𝚲 ̃(t) T , where 𝚺 𝛈 (𝑡) is the CF within time point covariance for some 𝛈 𝑡 .

Yet another possibly interesting scenario is when the dimension of the model varies over time.
For example, the model might 'collapse' towards singularity, i.e., the rank might shrink as the symptom process approaches a certain point.
Another possibility is that 𝚲(𝑡) might have a regime-switching property with the CF influencing symptoms at some time intervals, but not on other time intervals.
We note that when the number of CFs 𝑞 is time-varying 𝑞(𝑡), the model can be conceived as a model wherein 𝚲(𝑡) annihilates (sends to zero) a certain dimension of 𝛈 𝑡 .
I.e., when 𝚲(𝑡) is no longer a full column rank matrix, it reduces the dimension of the CF model and removes a CF by setting some CF to 0.
This model is indistinguishable from setting a CF to 0, or otherwise removing a CF, as the respective dimension is removed from the modelled symptoms in either case.
Likewise, 𝚲(𝑡) might at some other time point retain all 𝑞 CFs.
Therefore, in terms of indistinguishability between the SN and CF models, the time-varying CFs case can be considered as time-varying rank of 𝚲(𝑡).

text.text: We, at least heuristically, derive the result here so that the use of singular values in cross-covariance analysis is justified.

Continuous time preliminaries.
Remark 6: Continuous time pathwise indistinguishability.
We underline the differences and similarities between discrete and continuous time.

First, almost sure equality in terms of continuous time paths 20 ℙ({𝐗 𝑡 = 𝐙 𝑡 ∶ 𝑡 ∈ 𝒯}) = 1 is not a consequence of almost sure pointwise equivalence ℙ({𝐗 𝑡 = 𝐙 𝑡 }) = 1, for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝒯, which we have discussed so far for discrete time.
In general, the two equivalences are not the same.
However, whenever the processes are in discrete time or have almost surely continuous paths, the path and pointwise equivalence are the same.

Nevertheless, for the separate issue of indistinguishability in distribution it suffices to consider an arbitrary finite subset of time points 𝑠 1 , 𝑠 2 , … , 𝑠 𝑇 ∈ 𝒯 because 21 𝐗 𝑡 = 𝑑 𝐙 𝑡 ⇔ (𝐗 𝑠 1 , 𝐗 𝑠 2 , … , 𝐗 𝑠 𝑇 ) = 𝑑 (𝐙 𝑠 1 , 𝐙 𝑠 2 , … , 𝐙 𝑠 𝑇 ).
